before: The road out of the valley narrowed as it climbed, and by midday it had given up pretending to be a road at all. Mara walked it anyway.

She had been told the pass was closed. She had been told it three times, by three people who each had a reason to want her to stay: a farmer who wanted her hands through the harvest, a priest who wanted her confession, and a boy who only wanted her to stay. None of them had said what "closed" meant, exactly. Snow, probably. The word did so much work up here that nobody bothered to finish the sentence.
By the fourth switchback she understood. It was not snow that closed the pass. It was the quiet.
inserted: The road out of the valley narrowed as it climbed, and by midday it had given up pretending to be a road at all. Mara walked it anyway.

She had been told the pass was closed. She had been told it three times, by three people who each had a reason to want her to stay: a farmer who wanted her hands through the harvest, a priest who wanted her confession, and a boy who only wanted her to stay. None of them had said what "closed" meant, exactly. Snow, probably. The word did so much work up here that nobody bothered to finish the sentence.
By the fourth switchback she understood. It was not snow that closed the pass. It was the quiet.

Quiet in a valley is ordinary. Quiet at altitude is not. By the fourth switchback the wind had quit, and the river that ought to have been somewhere below her had stopped — or rather had gone on flowing without the courtesy of any sound. She stood still and listened, which was the only thing the priest had ever taught her that she still used.

She had come up this pass once before, in a summer, and it had been nothing but noise: water and wind and sheep bells, a fat man at the top selling fried dough to people who had earned it, arguing about the price. She had bought two and given one away.
Now there was nothing. No bird, no creak of pine, no shiver of gravel under a hoof. She counted her own footsteps for a while, the way you count coins when you suspect you have been cheated.
At the fifth switchback she found the bell.

It hung from a post driven into the scree, small and black with age, the sort you would tie to a goat. Someone had polished the inside of it, so the clean metal caught the light when she turned her head. She stood looking at it longer than the thing deserved.

It was strung between two pines across the trail, chest-high, and hung with flattened tin — lids and cans and one spoon, all of it punched through and threaded on. It was a warning. It was a warning built to be heard, which meant someone was meant to hear it, which meant someone was expected.

She could have turned back. There was a farmer in the valley who would have taken her in through the harvest and never asked a question she did not want to answer; there was a priest who would have taken her confession whether she wanted to give it or not; there was a boy who only wanted her to stay. Of the three he was the one she thought about, and the one she was least able to do it for.
She walked through the tin. It made no sound at all.

On the far side she picked up the spoon where it had fallen, considered it, and used it to strike the bell she had passed — one clean note, dropped into all that hush, gone, the way a stone goes into a well while you stand listening for the splash.
She was still listening when something above her on the slope heard it, and answered, and said her name.
